Minister confirms Ukraine has knocked back Australia's Tiger helicopters
The government has confirmed Ukraine has decided not to accept Australia's Tiger helicopters for defence against Russia's invasion.
Ukrainian media reports Kyiv believed the helicopter's maintenance requirements would outweigh the benefit of receiving the aircraft.
Anthony Albanese met with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last week.
Asked whether Australia is considering gifting Ukraine drones, cyber capabilities and missiles, Industry Minister Tim Ayres said he won't go into details.
But he points out that drone technology has been "critical" to Ukraine's defence.

"The decision from Ukraine not to take that technology from Australia is a decision for them. It is, as I understand it, based on their technical requirements and the way that it integrates with the rest of their systems," Ayres says.
"We will continue to find ways of supporting Ukraine, but I can't provide additional technical details or security details of the nature of that ongoing contribution."
Minns takes another swipe at federal Labor over spending
The NSW Premier Chris Minns has taken another veiled swipe at the federal government over its spending.
On Wednesday, the NSW Labor premier took a jab at the federal government over its spending, saying his state had been careful with public money.
He also declined to defend federal Labor's fiscal approach.
On the Future Women Leadership Series podcast, Minns warned that if the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates again, it risked tipping the economy into a recession.
He also doubled down on his comments, saying governments had a role to play in reducing spending, and that NSW felt the effects of interest rates more than other states.

"Interest rate rises in our economy are felt harder than anywhere else in the country, so NSW mortgage holders have to do the heavy lifting for demand in Western Australia or South Australia," Minns said.

"Government has got a role to play here too. We have worked really hard on being a commonsense, sensible government when it comes to public finances and we've got the lowest spending growth of any jurisdiction in the country."
Farrell suggests superannuation investment in US lamb industry to avoid more tariffs
Trade Minister Don Farrell has asked the Trump administration to consider sparing Australian sheep farmers from further tariff pain in exchange for Australian investment in the US lamb industry.
Farrell floated the idea, which could see Australians' superannuation savings invested in the American sector, during this week's G20 trade meetings in Milwaukee.
The proposal aims to get ahead of a US trade investigation into lamb imports, which could result in new tariffs.
Australian lamb exports to the US are already subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff, along with many other Australian products.
But American sheep producers, backed by dozens of Republican members of Congress, have been lobbying for tariffs specifically on sheep meat and wool from Australia and New Zealand.

Farrell's office has confirmed he discussed a possible lamb-industry "support package" with trade representative Jamieson Greer during the G20 event. Greer is a key architect of Donald Trump's tariff policies.

Shoebridge responds to Labor MP's Jewish 'prejudice' accusations
Greens leader David Shoebridge has responded to accusations from a Labor MP that he displayed "prejudice".

When asked at a press conference how he would repair the party's relationship with the Jewish community, Shoebridge said he had strong connections with Jewish Australians who were "fighting genocide", referring to the crisis in Gaza.
But Labor MP Josh Burns says Shoebridge's answer to the question is "shocking" and that people shouldn't be placed into categories based on their views.
Speaking to Channel Nine, Shoebridge has described Burns's position as "extraordinary".

"What I've said is there are so many progressive Jews who join with us in being horrified at the genocide that they're seeing in Gaza, horrified at what's happened in the name of the State of Israel," Shoebridge said.

"And the fact that when we say that there's this large part of the Jewish community who join with so many Australians in speaking out against the genocide, the fact that that is spun and twisted to suggest that's somehow divisive."
eSafety to act if gaming companies don't comply with child protection requirements
The eSafety commissioner says her agency is prepared to take action if big gaming companies fail to comply with age-assurance requirements.
The online safety watchdog has identified gaps in Roblox, Fortnite, Minecraft and Steam's protections for children.
Those gaps include harmful-content detection, repeat-offender prevention, and information-sharing initiatives.
"We've told them what their requirements are, and they're looking at the other privacy preserving age-assurance tools that they may be able to offer," Inman Grant says.
"We'll have to see what they actually deliver in the coming months. And we can always take formal enforcement action if they don't comply."
Labor targets migration lawyers and agents over 'futile' visa cases
Migration lawyers and agents who help people pursue baseless visa claims will be targeted under a federal government crackdown on those who profit from attempts to "game" the system.

Assistant Citizenship Minister Julian Hill will use a speech in Sydney on Friday to condemn professionals who sell "false hope" to clients with little prospect of remaining in Australia and flag plans to restrict their activity.
Hill will also unveil more details of Labor's broader migration overhaul announced last month, including that new restrictions on international students will take effect from today.
Australia's net overseas migration (NOM) was 292,100 in the year to March, with the government pledging to reduce the rate to 225,000 by next financial year.

Malinauskas defends federal government spending after NSW premier's comments
SA Premier Peter Malinauskas has pushed back on the suggestion the federal government isn't doing enough to rein in spending.
On Wednesday, NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns took a swipe at the federal government over its spending, saying his state has been careful with public money.
But Malinauskas has defended the federal government on ABC Radio National Breakfast, saying states "aren't immune from scrutiny".

"All too often the critique is made in the absence of any thoughtful suggestion about what should be cut. I mean, is it the Commonwealth government investment in Medicare or education services? I mean, I don't think that would be particularly good for the country," Malinauskas says.
Ayres says government's focus with Bell Bay $200m bailout was securing jobs
Industry Minister Tim Ayres has evaded questions about why taxpayers won't see much return from the Bell Bay aluminium bailout.
The Australian and Tasmanian governments yesterday announced a $200 million package for the Bell Bay aluminium smelter in Tasmania.
The package was delayed because the smelter's owner, Rio Tinto, had been locked in protracted negotiations with the state-owned power company Hydro Tasmania over a new power deal.
Ayres has sidestepped questions about why the power deal was only for five years, when other comparable power agreements are for 10 years.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Ayres says the government's focus was about securing jobs in northern Tasmania.

"The overwhelming objective here is to secure these 550 jobs, 1,000 indirect jobs, in what is a part of Australia where these blue-collar jobs are really not just really important here but there's this capability here that can make Australia's economy stronger," Ayres says.
Hume calls on ATO to reverse credit card payment ban
Deputy Liberal Leader Jane Hume has urged the government to reverse the tax office's decision to stop accepting credit card payments.
From yesterday, businesses were banned from adding a surcharge to customers using electronic terminals to pay for goods on card networks including eftpos, Mastercard and Visa.
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has also announced it will stop accepting credit card payments from November 30 because of the surcharge ban.
Some businesses have increased prices after the ban to cover bank and card fees.
Speaking to Channel Seven, Hume says customers will ultimately have to pay more.

"The Coalition is calling on the government to reverse this change that the ATO is imposing on small businesses, because, quite frankly, it's been very clear that this government doesn't understand small business and it's imposing unnecessary costs on them," Hume says.
Appearing on the same panel, Wentworth MP Allegra Spender says she'll write to the ATO to ask it to reverse the ban on accepting credit card payments.
Cutting corporate tax rate could help lift productivity, Productivity Commission says
The Productivity Commission says its proposal to cut the company tax rate would help with Australia's productivity challenge.
The commission has previously called for a 20 per cent tax rate on profits for companies with revenue of up to $1 billion, but it was never adopted in May's federal budget.
On Tuesday, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said productivity was "doing nothing", and that stronger productivity would allow more to be produced without adding to inflation.
Angela Jackson, from the Productivity Commission, says cutting corporate tax rates is one of the easiest ways to lift productivity.
"We want to ensure that all the settings are encouraging business investment," Jackson says.

"We did look at the real drop-off that we've seen since the GFC [Global Financial Crisis] in business investment and what we could do to lift that. Company tax reform is one of the sort of the easiest ways, if you like, pathways to doing that."
Leeser calls on PM, minister to visit WA over child protection concerns
Shadow Indigenous Australians Minister Julian Leeser has called for federal agencies to get involved in cases of unsupervised children in WA in state care.
Up to 15 Aboriginal children, some as young as five, were living unsupervised in a state-owned home in South Hedland.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Leeser says services across the state and federal government have failed to coordinate.
He says there has been a failure of welfare checks, and has called on the PM and the federal Indigenous Australians minister to visit the area.

"The state government now has set up a coordination committee. It doesn't include the federal agencies. I'd like to see the federal agencies involved as well. And I'd like to see the federal minister and the prime minister visit there too," Leeser says.

Gaming giants told to 'lift their game' on child safety
Australia's online safety watchdog has taken aim at some of the world's biggest gaming companies, telling them to step up their protections for children.

After reviewing their submissions, the eSafety Commission found big differences in how Roblox, Fortnite, Minecraft and Steam deal with serious harms including grooming, child exploitation, and violent extremist content.
It identified gaps in harmful content detection, repeat-offender prevention, and information-sharing initiatives.
Age checks remain a big issue, with both Fortnite and Minecraft largely relying on users to declare their ages, making it harder to apply age-based protections.
Valve was singled out as the only platform not using hash-matching, a technology that helps to quickly detect and identify child sexual abuse material.
eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant says while there's been some improvement to prevent serious harms, she expects services to "lift their game".

"Australian children have a right to play online without being exposed to predators, sexual extortionists, violent extremist content or other harmful material," Inman Grant says."Service providers should leverage systems that actually detect and disrupt serious harms before children are exposed to them."

This is the first time a gaming audit has taken place under the Online Safety Act, with the proposed Digital Duty of Care bill shifting further emphasis to how platforms prevent harm.
